facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 a public demonstration entitled the 'March of Millions' was held in central Moscow.
The march on 6 May 2012 was peaceful and held without any disruptions.
The applicant took part in the demonstration on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square.
The applicant was arrested at the venue of the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
After her arrest at Bolotnaya Square, the applicant was taken to a police station.
At the police station, the applicant was charged with an administrative offence.
After a night in detention, the applicant was released.
On 8 May 2012 the applicant was convicted of the administrative offence with which she had been charged.
On 8 May 2012 the applicant was exempted from administrative liability.
According to the applicant, on 6 May 2012 she participated in the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square.
According to the applicant, she conducted herself peacefully at the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
According to the applicant, she did not take part in any acts of violence prior to her arrest at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
According to the applicant, at 6 p.m. on 6 May 2012 she was arrested by the police at Bolotnaya Square.
According to the applicant, at around 9 p.m. on 6 May 2012 she was taken to Taganskiy district police station of Moscow.
According to the Government, the applicant was arrested at 6 p.m. on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square.
According to the Government, the applicant was arrested because she had been participating in breaking the police cordon at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
According to the Government, at 7.20 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the applicant was taken to Taganskiy district police station.

According to the Government, the time of 7.20 p.m. on 6 May 2012 as the time the applicant was taken to Taganskiy district police station was also indicated in the record of her transfer to the police station for the purpose of compiling an administrative file.
According to the Government, the applicant was released on 7 May 2012.
The record of administrative arrest indicated that the applicant had been arrested at 8.45 p.m. at the police station.
The record of administrative arrest contained no mention of the date or time of the applicant's release.
The record of administrative arrest indicated that the applicant had not asked to notify anyone of her arrest.
The applicant signed an undertaking that she would attend court if ordered by the judge to do so.

After the applicant's arrest, an on-duty officer drew up an administrative-offence record on the basis of the reports and explanatory notes of police officers G.S. and M.S., who had arrested the applicant.
The reports and explanatory notes of police officers G.S. and M.S. were drawn up using an identical template.
The reports and explanatory notes of police officers G.S. and M.S. contained no individualised information except the police officers' personal information and the applicant's name.
The applicant was accused of disobeying lawful orders of the police, an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The administrative-offence record reiterated the reports and notes of police officers G.S. and M.S.
The administrative-offence record stated that the applicant, acting as part of a group of 1,500 citizens, took part in an authorised meeting.
The administrative-offence record stated that during the event the applicant committed a breach of the rules on holding public events by breaking the police cordon.

The administrative-offence record stated that by breaking the police cordon the applicant prevented police officers from carrying out their service duties, in breach of Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
According to the applicant, at the police station she was not allowed to make a phone call, despite making insistent requests.
According to the applicant, she told the police at the police station that she was the mother of a fifteen-month-old child left at home with a babysitter.
According to the applicant, she requested that her family be notified of her arrest, but this was refused by the police.
According to the applicant, her passport contained no information about her baby.
According to the applicant, at the police station she was detained in a small overcrowded cell with no sanitary facilities, sleeping place or bedding.
According to the applicant, she had no access to drinking water at the police station.
According to the applicant, she was given no food at the police station.
The administrative case file contained an explanatory note by the applicant.
In her explanatory note, the applicant stated that during the demonstration she had happened to be in the middle of the crowd, which had pulled her towards the police officers.
In her explanatory note, the applicant stated that at some point she had been arrested and taken to the police station, even though she had not chanted any slogans.
At around 6 p.m. on 7 May 2012 the applicant appeared before a justice of the peace.
The applicant's administrative case could not be examined on 7 May 2012 and she was taken back to the police station.
According to the applicant, she was released from the police station at about 10 p.m. on 7 May 2012.
The applicant signed an undertaking that she would attend the court hearing of the administrative case.
On 8 May 2012 the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District examined the charges against the applicant.

On the basis of the police officers' reports and explanations and the records of administrative transfer and arrest, the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District established that the applicant had committed an administrative offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as described in the administrative-offence record.
At the hearing on 8 May 2012, the applicant repeated the statements she had given in her explanatory note.
The applicant's statements at the hearing on 8 May 2012 were dismissed by the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District.

The Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District decided to absolve the applicant from administrative liability on the grounds that her offence had not entailed serious consequences.
The Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District decided to absolve the applicant from administrative liability on the grounds that she had a baby born in 2011.
The Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District issued the applicant a warning.
The applicant did not appeal against the judgment of the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of 8 May 2012.
On 26 July 2012 the applicant lodged a complaint under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure with the Dorogomilovskiy District Court of Moscow.
The applicant's complaint of 26 July 2012 concerned her allegedly arbitrary arrest on 6 May 2012 and detention until 7 May 2012.
The applicant's complaint of 26 July 2012 concerned the termination of the rally at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
The applicant's complaint of 26 July 2012 concerned the conditions of her detention at the police station.

On 3 September 2012 the Dorogomilovskiy District Court of Moscow refused to examine the applicant's complaint on the grounds that the contested acts of the police had been the matter of the administrative proceedings and could not be challenged separately.
On 3 September 2012 the Dorogomilovskiy District Court of Moscow did not examine the applicant's complaint about the conditions of detention.

On 20 May 2013 the Moscow City Court quashed the part of the Dorogomilovskiy District Court's decision of 3 September 2012 concerning the refusal to examine the complaint about the conditions of detention.
On 20 May 2013 the Moscow City Court upheld the remaining part of the Dorogomilovskiy District Court's decision of 3 September 2012.
On 23 October 2013 the Dorogomilovskiy District Court dismissed the applicant's complaint about the conditions of her detention at the police station as unsubstantiated.
On 28 February 2014 the Moscow City Court upheld the Dorogomilovskiy District Court's judgment of 23 October 2013 dismissing the applicant's complaint about the conditions of her detention.
For a summary of the relevant domestic law, see Frumkin v. Russia (no. 74568/12, §§ 77 and 79, 5 January 2016).
Article 3.9 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences provides that administrative detention may not be applied to women with children under fourteen years old.

According to Article 2.9 of the Code of Administrative Offences, a judge examining an administrative case may exempt an offender from administrative liability and issue a warning if the offence was minor.
Paragraph 1.1 (2) of Article 29.9 of the Code of Administrative Offences stipulates that if a warning is issued, the administrative proceedings must be discontinued.

Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure (in force until 15 September 2015) described the procedure for examining complaints about decisions, acts or omissions of State and municipal authorities and officials.

Article 254 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Chapter 25, in force until 15 September 2015) provided that a person could lodge a complaint with a court about an act or decision by any State or municipal authority or official if he or she considered that the act or decision had violated his or her rights and freedoms.

Article 255 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Chapter 25, in force until 15 September 2015) provided that the complaint could concern any decision, act or omission which had violated the person's rights or freedoms, had impeded their exercise, or had imposed a duty or liability on that person.

Article 256 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Chapter 25, in force until 15 September 2015) provided that the complaint had to be lodged with a court of general jurisdiction within three months of the date on which the complainant had learnt of the breach of his rights.

In Ruling no. 2 of 10 February 2009, the Plenary Supreme Court of Russia stated that the procedure under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not applicable to challenges against actions, omissions or decisions for which the Code of Administrative Offences did not establish a review procedure and which, being intrinsically linked to a given case of administrative offence charges, were not amenable to a separate review (paragraph 7 of the Ruling).

In Ruling no. 2 of 10 February 2009, the Plenary Supreme Court of Russia stated that the above statement was relevant for evidence in cases where certain measures were recorded, for instance in a record of transfer to a police station or a record of administrative arrest.

In Ruling no. 2 of 10 February 2009, the Plenary Supreme Court of Russia stated that in circumstances where measures were recorded in a record of transfer to a police station or a record of administrative arrest, arguments relating to the inadmissibility of a piece of evidence or measure could be presented during examination of the administrative offence case or on appeal against a decision in such a case.

In Ruling no. 2 of 10 February 2009, the Plenary Supreme Court of Russia stated that where administrative proceedings were discontinued, any actions taken during the proceedings could then be challenged under Chapter 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, if they impinged upon the person's rights or freedoms, created obstacles to their being exercised, or imposed liability unlawfully.
